'''''Pseudognaphalium luteoalbum''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] including '''''Helichrysum luteoalbum''''',  is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[family (botany)|family]] [[Asteraceae]]. In the [[United Kingdom]], it is known as the '''Jersey cudweed'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref>

==Description==
It is an erect [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|biennial]] up to {{convert|70|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall, branching from the base. Leaves are [[oblanceolate]] to lanceolate and covered in hairs like that of the [[edelweiss]]. The leaves can survive freezing in winter. Flowers are cream, yellow, white, or pink.<ref name="FloraBase 29594">{{FloraBase | name = ''Helichrysum luteoalbum'' (L.) Rchb. | id = 29594}}</ref> Seeds have a [[pappus (botany)|pappus]] which lets them float over long distances.

==Taxonomy==
This species was first published by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his 1753 ''[[Species plantarum]]'', under the name ''Gnaphalium luteo-album'' (the orthography was later changed to omit the hyphen). In 1829, [[Ludwig Reichenbach]] transferred it to ''[[Helichrysum]]'', but this name was not taken up, and the species was retained in ''[[Gnaphalium]]'' until 1981, when [[Olive Mary Hilliard]] and [[Brian Laurence Burtt]] transferred it into ''[[Pseudognaphalium]]''.<ref name="APNI 60679">{{APNI | name = ''Gnaphalium luteoalbum'' L. | id = 60679}}</ref><ref name="APNI 33305">{{APNI | name = ''Pseudognaphalium luteoalbum'' (L.) Hilliard & B. L.Burtt | id = 33305}}</ref>

In 2004, an investigation into the phylogenetic relationships of ''Helichrysum'' and related genera found this species to have arisen within ''Helichrysum''. As a result of this, Reichenbach's long-forgotten name for this species was resurrected.<ref name="Galbany-Casals 2004">{{cite journal | author = Galbany-Casals, M.| year = 2004 | title = Phylogenetic relationships in the Mediterranean ''Helichrysum'' (Asteraceae, Gnaphalieae) based on nuclear rDNA ITS sequence data | journal = Australian Systematic Botany | volume = 17 | issue = 3 | pages = 241–253 | doi = 10.1071/SB03031|display-authors=etal}}</ref> A later study suggested that all the sampled ''[[Pseudognaphalium]]'' species arose within ''[[Helichrysum]]'' as did ''[[Anaphalis]]'', ''[[Achyrocline]]'' and ''[[Humeocline]]''.<ref>Galbany-Casals, M.; et al. Phylogenetic relationships in Helichrysum (Compositae: Gnaphalieae) and related genera: Incongruence between nuclear and plastid phylogenies, biogeographic and morphological patterns, and implications for generic delimitation. 2014. ''Taxon''. 63(3):608-624</ref> Subsequent phylogenetic studies showed that ''Helichrysum'', ''Anaphalis'' and ''Pseudognaphalium'' formed a clade, but retained these genera.<ref name=SchmBovi21>{{Citation |last1=Schmidt-Lebuhn |first1=Alexander N. |last2=Bovill |first2=Jessica |date=2021 |title=Phylogenomic data reveal four major clades of Australian Gnaphalieae (Asteraceae) |journal=Taxon |volume=70 |issue=5 |pages=1020–1034 |doi=10.1002/tax.12510 |name-list-style=amp }}</ref>

The [[botanical Latin]] [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''luteoalbum'' translates as 'pale yellow'.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This species is so widely distributed that it is unclear where it is native and where naturalised. In general it is considered naturalised in [[North America|North]] and [[South America]], and native to every other continent except Antarctica.<ref name="GRIN 411038">{{GRIN | name = ''Pseudognaphalium luteoalbum'' (L.) Hilliard & B. L. Burtt | id = 411038}}</ref> It grows in meadows, wastelands, and edges of forests. Its rosettes are occasionally mistaken for edelweiss.

==Uses==
In Vietnam, the plant is used as a food ingredient, such as in the rice cake ''banh khuc''. It has also been used in traditional medicine of the region, as a diuretic, hemostatic, antipyretic, for the treatment of cough, and for pain relief.<ref>{{ cite book | first1=Yoshitaka | last1=Tanaka | first2=Nguyen | last2=Van Ke | date=2007 | title=Edible Wild Plants of Vietnam: The Bountiful Garden | publisher=Thailand: Orchid Press | isbn=978-9745240896 | page=47}}</ref>
